content:
We have now studied the vessels of the dedication offering; the silver plate,
the silver bowl, and the golden spoon. We have walked through the burnt offering animals; the young bull of total strength and surrender, the ram of substitution, the one-year-old lamb pointing to the Passover and all the ages of God’s plan. And we have seen how the number thirty-six across all the burnt offerings carries the weight of broken covenant reversed by the complete obedience of Christ. Today we come to the fourth offering that each tribal leader brought: the sin offering. Numbers 7:16 says simply: “one kid of the goats for a sin offering.” One. A single male goat. No variation, no addition. Just one goat, every time, for every tribe, over all twelve days.

Before we can understand why a goat was chosen for the sin offering and what it points to in Christ, we need to understand what the goat represented in the language of Israel’s sacrificial system. The goat was not the animal of celebration or fellowship. It was not the ox of covenant feasting or the lamb of the Passover table. The goat was the animal of the Day of Atonement; the most solemn, most weighty day in all of Israel’s calendar. Leviticus 16 describes how on the Day of Atonement two goats were brought before Yahweh. One was sacrificed as a sin offering and its blood was taken by the high priest into the Most Holy Place to be sprinkled on the Mercy Seat. The other; the scapegoat had the sins of all Israel confessed over it by the high priest, and then it was led away into the wilderness, bearing all the iniquity of the people, never to return.

The two goats of the Day of Atonement together painted the complete picture of what atonement means. The first goat said: the penalty for sin is death, and the blood must be brought before the face of Yahweh in the place of the guilty. The second goat said: and then the sin is taken away, carried off, removed from the sight of God, sent so far away that it never returns. One goat for the penalty. One goat for the removal. Together they said what no single animal could say alone. And when Christ came, He fulfilled both. Hebrews 9:12 says He entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood; the first goat. And Hebrews 9:26 says He appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of Himself. He was both. The penalty paid and the sin removed, in one person, on one cross, once.

The specific offering of a male goat for a sin offering was not unusual in Israel’s worship life. Leviticus 4:22-26 gives the instruction for when a leader sinned unintentionally: he was to bring a male goat as a sin offering. And Leviticus 4:13-21 gives the instruction for when the whole congregation of Israel sinned unintentionally: a young bull was brought for the congregation’s sin offering. But in Numbers 15:24, when the whole congregation erred, the sin offering alongside the burnt offering included a male goat. The male goat was the animal of representative, covering sin; used for leaders and for the congregation together, pointing to an offering that could stand on behalf of all.

Now consider what Christ did. He did not die for one tribe. He did not make atonement for one generation only. Isaiah 53:6 says: “All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned, every one, to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on Him the iniquity of us all.” All. Everyone. The iniquity of us all. The male goat of the sin offering in Numbers 7 was brought by each of the twelve leaders, representing each of the twelve tribes. Every tribe needed a sin offering.
Not one tribe was exempt from the need for atonement. The goat stood before the altar on behalf of every person in that tribe; from the greatest leader to the least child. And Christ stood before the cross on behalf of every person in all the tribes of the whole human family; the one true sin offering who could bear what no animal could truly carry.

The most important verse about the sin offering in the New Testament is
2 Corinthians 5:21: “For our sake He made Him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.” He made Him to be sin. Not a sinner. Not like a sinner. He was the Sin offering; the entire weight and reality of human sin was placed on Him. The goat of the sin offering had done nothing wrong. It had no guilt of its own. It was clean and without blemish. But it was brought to the altar and killed in the place of those who were guilty. Christ had done nothing wrong. He was without sin, without blemish, without any inward or outward corruption. But He was brought to the cross and died in the place of those who were guilty. The exchange was total and real.

Hebrews 13:11-13 shows us another dimension of this: “For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp. So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through His own blood.” Certain sin offering animals were not treated like the other sacrifices. It was taken outside the camp and burned there. It was removed from the place of fellowship and worship because it had become identified with the sin it was carrying.

And Christ was crucified outside the city; outside the gate, outside the camp, in the place of rejection and shame. He went where the sin offering had gone. He died outside so that those who were outside could come inside. He bore the shame of the camp’s exterior so that the guilty could enter the sanctuary.

This is what each tribal leader was declaring when he brought the one male goat to the altar of dedication. He was saying: my tribe is guilty. We have sinned. We cannot stand before Yahweh on our own goodness. We need a substitute who will bear what we cannot carry and go to the place we deserve to go. And twelve leaders, twelve goats, twelve days, twelve declarations of the same truth: we need the one true sin offering who is coming. Tomorrow we will look at why there was only one goat; and what the singularity of that offering says to a world that believes there are many ways to deal with sin.

title: Prayer
text:
Yahweh, You are the Holy One of Israel; You are our King and Saviour (Isaiah 43:15). You are the God whose holiness required atonement and whose love provided it. We thank You for the male goat of the sin offering; for every time it was placed on the altar of Israel’s worship as a declaration that sin is real, that it has a cost, and that a substitute must bear what the guilty cannot bear.

We thank You that Christ fulfilled both goats of the Day of Atonement in one sacrifice; that the penalty was paid and the sin was carried away, both in Him, both on the same cross, both settled once and for all. Forgive us for treating the sin offering as ordinary, for coming before You as though the cross were a detail rather than the centre of everything. Let the weight of 2 Corinthians 5:21 rest on us today: He was made a sin offerings for us. In Christ’s name, amen.
